title: Americans Are Negative About Social Media’s Impact on Democracy – and the Rest of the World Is Catching Up
summary: In 2026, 64% of Americans say social media is harming their democracy, and attitudes in many other countries are significantly more negative than they used to be.

title: Social Media Platform Use Around the World
summary: Facebook is generally the top platform globally, followed by Instagram, while fewer overall use TikTok, X or Snapchat.

title: Across the Globe, People Increasingly Say Social Media Is Harming Democracy
summary: Most think social media leads to manipulation and division, but they also say it informs people and gives them a voice in politics.

title: From cash to credit, how Americans’ payment methods have changed in the past decade
summary: Since 2015, the share of Americans who say they use cash for all or almost all of their purchases in a typical week has fallen by half, from 24% to 12%.

title: How synthetic polling results change based on the AI model
summary: Survey experiments with Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.1 each paint a very different picture of U.S. public opinion, neither of which reflect reality.

title: How well synthetic polls capture the diversity of public opinion
summary: AI survey respondents are more likely than humans to agree on one answer choice or avoid a response option entirely.

title: Synthetic surveys and ‘timely and topical’ questions
summary: Synthetic surveys fail to replicate public opinion on timely and topical issues in early 2026, including presidential approval and views of data centers.

title: How synthetic respondents express certainty and factual knowledge
summary: AI survey respondents are far less likely than humans to select "not sure" or factually incorrect answers.

title: How well synthetic samples replicate public opinion
summary: Synthetic survey respondents tend to exaggerate differences between demographic subgroups and portray some responses as nearly universal.

title: Can AI Stand In for Human Survey-Takers? Not Really
summary: Synthetic surveys using digital twins do a poor job estimating the public mood and are especially error-prone for some subgroups, including Republicans and Black adults.
